_what: The terms on /glossary, rendered by src/pages/[...slug].astro in this order. Plain definitions of words a reviewer, lender, leasing office or credit bureau uses; no advice and no outcome promises.

terms.definition: A short, signed note that explains one thing a reviewer asked about, such as a late payment, a job gap or a large deposit, in plain words with the dates and the proof attached.
Documents that show what you earn and from where: pay stubs, a W-2 or 1099 form, tax returns, a benefits award letter, or bank statements showing regular deposits.

A check that you work where you say you do, usually covering your job title, start date and pay. It may come as a letter your employer signs, a form the lender sends, or a third-party verification service.
A period between jobs. A reviewer may ask for its dates and the reason, usually in a short letter of explanation.
Your monthly debt payments divided by your gross monthly income, shown as a percentage. Lenders use it to judge how much of your income is already committed.
The lender's review of an application: income, assets, credit and documents are checked before a loan decision is made. The person doing it is the underwriter.
Items an underwriter still needs before a loan can close, such as a missing document or a letter of explanation. Each condition is cleared by sending what it asks for.
A deposit on a bank statement that is bigger than your usual pattern. A lender may ask you to show where it came from with a document and a short explanation.
A signed statement from someone giving you money toward a home purchase, saying the money is a gift and does not have to be repaid. It is signed by the person giving the gift.
The record of where you have rented, for how long and how you paid. A leasing office may check it with past landlords or ask for a landlord reference letter.
A second person who agrees to be responsible for the rent or the loan if you do not pay. A leasing office or lender may ask for one when your own income or credit does not meet its rules.
A company that keeps credit reports: Equifax, Experian and TransUnion are the three nationwide ones. The law calls them consumer reporting agencies.
Your written request that a credit bureau, or the company that reported an item, investigate information you believe is wrong. Disputing an error with a bureau is free.

The company that sends information about your account to a credit bureau, such as a lender, card issuer or collection agency. You can dispute an item with the furnisher directly as well as with the bureau.
A letter asking a creditor to reconsider how it reported a late payment that really happened. It asks for a courtesy; it does not claim an error, and the creditor may say no.
A letter asking a debt collector to show the details of a debt it is collecting, such as the amount and the original creditor.
Tools that help you prepare your own paperwork. They do not fix credit for you, and they never contact a bureau or creditor on your behalf.
A one-time ApprovalPrep download for one situation: a PDF guide plus an editable Word file of letters and checklists you fill in and send yourself.
